title: Resort Photography and Video That Help Win Bookings
excerpt: Shot lists per room type, what guests look for in resort photos, honest editing, Reels footage and how to use one approved image set across OTAs, Google and your website.
description: Resort photography and video for bookings: shot lists per room type, honest editing, Reels footage and one image set across OTAs and your website.
html:
Resort photography that wins bookings shows each room type honestly and completely: the bed, the bathroom, the view from the window, the space around the room, and the meals and common areas guests will use. Plan a shot list per room type, keep editing natural, and use one approved image set across your website, Google listing and every OTA.

What guests actually scrutinise in resort photos

Guests flick quickly through the first few images, then slow down on the ones that help them decide. In practice, that usually means:

  • The bed and room size: is it a real king bed, is there space for an extra bed or a child?
  • The bathroom: cleanliness, shower or tub, hot water fittings. This is where many guests look for signs of age.
  • The view: what they will see from the bed or balcony, not from a drone.
  • Room differences: why the "Premium Cottage" costs more than the "Deluxe Room".
  • Food: the actual breakfast spread or thali, not stock images.
  • Pool and common areas: size, shade, whether children can use them.
  • Getting there: the approach road, parking, steps for older guests.

If a guest cannot answer these from your photos, they either message you, which is fine, or move on to a listing that answers them, which is not.

A shot list per room type

Give your photographer a written list for every room category. Shoot each room type in the same way so guests can compare.

ShotWhat it showsTip
Wide room from the doorwayOverall size and layoutShoot at chest height, not from a corner on the floor
Bed with side tablesBed size, linen, lightingMake the bed as housekeeping normally does
Opposite wallSeating, wardrobe, TV, deskShows what the wide shot hides
Bathroom wideShower, basin, toilet layoutTurn on all lights, dry all surfaces
Bathroom detailFittings, toiletriesOnly what every guest receives
View from the bed or balconyWhat the guest actually seesShoot from inside the room as well as outside
Balcony or sit-outPrivate outdoor spaceInclude chairs at real scale
Exterior of the cottage or blockWhere the room sits on the propertyHelps guests understand privacy and stairs
Extra bed or family setupHow the room works for fourNeeded if you sell family occupancy

Then shoot the property-wide set: entrance and approach, reception, restaurant with real food, pool at different times, activity areas, meeting space if you sell offsites, and the countryside around the property.

Honest images versus over-edited ones

Heavy editing creates a short-term gain and a long-term problem. Guests who arrive to find a smaller room, a greyer sky and a cloudier pool than the photos promised write reviews about it. Those reviews then cost more bookings than the edited photos won.

Acceptable edits

  • Correcting exposure and white balance so colours match reality.
  • Straightening lines and fixing lens distortion.
  • Removing temporary clutter such as a housekeeping trolley or a stray cable.
  • Blending exposures so the window view and the room interior are both visible.

Edits to avoid

  • Replacing skies or adding sunsets that were not there.
  • Ultra-wide lenses that make a small room look twice its size.
  • Removing permanent features such as a nearby building or power lines.
  • Turning a green-brown river blue, or a dry lawn bright green.
  • Using photos of a renovated room to represent rooms that have not been renovated.

A useful rule: if a guest would be surprised on arrival, the photo is misleading. Your reviews will tell you whether you have got this right; the reputation management guide in this series shows how to track that theme.

Timing, seasons and people in shots

Shoot in the season you most want to sell, and update when the property looks very different at other times. A Kerala property in monsoon and in January can look like two places; some properties show both, honestly labelled.

Early morning and late afternoon light suit exteriors. Interiors are usually best mid-morning with all lights on. People help guests imagine the stay, but use real guests only with written permission, or staff and friends who have agreed, and keep them natural rather than posed.

Video and Reels assets

Short vertical video is now part of the same asset set. While the photographer is on site, capture video too, so you are not organising a second shoot.

  • A 15 to 30 second room walk-through for each room type, from door to balcony, in one steady take.
  • A short arrival clip: the approach, the gate, reception, the first view.
  • Food being served, not just plated.
  • Activities in progress: a plantation walk, a bonfire, a kayak launch.
  • Ambient clips of 5 to 10 seconds each: rain on the roof, morning mist, the pool at dusk.

Shoot vertically for Reels and stories, and horizontally where you need website or YouTube clips. Record natural sound; it often works better than music. The post on resort Instagram and Reels content shows how to build a calendar from this footage.

One asset set across OTAs and your website

The same guest often sees your resort on several platforms before booking. If MakeMyTrip shows renovated rooms, Booking.com shows the old ones, and your website shows a different set again, it looks careless and raises doubt.

  1. Create a master folder with approved images, named by room type and shot, such as "family-cottage-01-wide.jpg".
  2. Pick a lead order: the first five images every platform should show, matched to your positioning.
  3. Upload the same set to your website, Google Business Profile, every OTA and Airbnb.
  4. Tag images by room type on OTAs that allow it, so guests see the right photos for each category.
  5. Log the date of the shoot and plan a refresh after any renovation.

Which images lead depends on who the resort is for; that decision is covered in resort brand positioning. Make sure your website loads these images quickly on mobile, which our web design and development team handles through compression and sizing.

Frequently asked questions

How many photos should each room type have?

Enough to answer the main questions without repetition: typically a wide shot, the bed, the opposite wall, the bathroom, the view and any balcony or sit-out, plus a family setup if you sell it. That is usually six to ten images per room type. Beyond that, extra angles add little; it is more useful to cover the restaurant, pool and approach properly.

Is a phone good enough for resort photography?

Modern phones can produce usable images, especially for social media and quick updates. For your main listing set, a professional photographer with interiors experience is usually worth it, because lighting, lens choice and composition affect how accurately rooms come across. Use the phone for regular Reels and stories, and the professional set for OTAs, Google and the website.

Should resort photos include people?

A few, yes. People in the pool, at breakfast or on an activity help guests picture themselves there and show scale. Keep them natural and relevant to your main audience. Use only people who have given written permission, and avoid identifiable children unless parents have explicitly agreed. Room shots generally work better without people, so guests can see the space clearly.

How often should a resort update its photos?

Update after any renovation, new room type, change in furnishings or significant landscaping change, and whenever reviews suggest the photos no longer match reality. Otherwise, a full refresh every two or three years keeps the set current. Seasonal images, such as monsoon greenery or winter mist, can be added between full shoots, clearly labelled.

Where to start

Open your listing on two OTAs and your website side by side and note where the photos differ or look dated. Write a shot list per room type using the table above. Book one shoot that covers stills and vertical video, then upload the same approved set everywhere in the same order.
